opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting thing it makes possible is lowering the barrier between having a problem and having a model that solves it.

Right now, if you're a biologist or a materials scientist or a small business owner and you have a very specific need, say predicting some property from your own experimental data, you basically have two options. You either learn a lot of machine learning yourself, or you find an ML engineer, explain your domain to them, and go back and forth for months. A lot of valuable problems never get solved, not because they're hard, but because the translation cost is too high.

A system that takes requirements in natural language, like "here's my data, I care about interpretability, it has to run on a cheap device, and I need it to respect this physical constraint," and then handles architecture design, training, tuning, and deployment, collapses that translation cost. It's a bit like what compilers did for programming. People stopped writing assembly and started describing what they wanted at a higher level.

My own interests add a second layer to this. I care a lot about science and interpretability, so I'd want such a system to produce not just a black box that scores well but models people can understand. Ideally it would sometimes hand you back a symbolic formula or a small, structured model and say, "this is what your data seems to be telling you." Then it's a tool for discovery, not just automation.

There are real challenges. Requirements are often vague, and users don't always know what they want until they see something. Evaluation is hard: how does the system know the model is actually good and not just overfitting some benchmark it set for itself? And there are safety and reliability questions once you let a system deploy things automatically. So I think the near-term version is more of a collaborator than a fully autonomous engineer, where the human stays in the loop on what "good" means.

But if we get it right, I think it means many more people get to do the kind of modeling that today only well-resourced labs can do, and that could speed up science quite a lot.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it would change who gets to be a scientist, more than it would change what AI is.

Right now, if you want to build a model for some narrow problem, say predicting how a protein folds under some unusual condition, or finding patterns in a small physics dataset, you need a lot of implicit knowledge. Which architecture, which optimizer, what learning rate schedule, how to debug when the loss goes flat. That knowledge lives in a few thousand people's heads, mostly in a handful of labs. So the questions that get answered are the questions those people find interesting. A system that takes a requirement in plain language and returns a trained, deployed model removes that bottleneck. A biologist or an economist could ask a question in their own terms and get a tool back the same day.

But I want to be careful, because I come at this from physics, and in physics the model is never the point. The point is understanding. If the system just hands you a black box that fits your data, you've gained a prediction and lost the chance to learn something. So the version of this I actually care about is one where the design process is itself legible. The system should be able to tell you why it chose a sparse architecture, or that your data has a symmetry it exploited, or that a simple formula explains ninety percent of the variance and the neural net is only cleaning up the rest. That's what we were trying to get at with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, making the learned functions readable so a human can look and recognize a sine or a logarithm.

If you combine those two things, automation plus interpretability, then I think you get something genuinely new. Not just more models, but a kind of collaborator that does the tedious parts of science and hands the interesting parts back to you. Hypothesis generation at scale, where every hypothesis comes with a trained model and a readable explanation. That's the possibility that excites me.

The thing that worries me is the opposite failure mode. If the system optimizes only for the user's stated metric, it will happily produce models that are brittle, that cheat on distribution shift, that no one understands. Automation amplifies whatever objective you give it. So the quality of the requirement specification becomes the whole game, and most people are not good at specifying what they actually want. I think we'll spend a lot of the next few years learning that lesson.

astra-6.text:
I think it could make building AI much more accessible. Today, even if you know exactly what problem you want to solve, you still need expertise to choose a model, prepare the data, train it, and deploy it. A system like that could let you describe your goal and constraints—how accurate it needs to be, how fast it should run, what resources you have—and turn those into a working solution.

It could also make experimentation much faster. You could try an idea, see where it fails, and refine your requirements. But the key is whether the system can check that it actually solved your problem. Training a model successfully doesn’t necessarily mean it’s useful in practice. So I’d want it to ask clarifying questions, evaluate the results, and make its limitations clear. That would let people spend more time deciding which problems are worth solving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could make building AI much more accessible. Today, even if you know exactly what problem you want to solve, you still need expertise in choosing a model, preparing data, training it, and deploying it. A system like that could let you start by describing the outcome you want and the constraints you have—your budget, the accuracy you need, or how quickly it must respond.

That could allow a scientist, a teacher, or a small business owner to build tools for very specific needs without assembling an entire machine learning team. It could also make experimentation much faster: you could try an idea, see where it fails, and refine your requirements.

But the important part is whether the system can check that it has actually solved your problem. Training a model is only one step. It also needs to recognize when the data is insufficient, ask clarifying questions, and communicate its limitations. If it can do those things reliably, it could turn AI development into a much more collaborative process.
